children: Prominent US plaintiffs law firm Morgan & Morgan cannot sue to block Florida’s restrictions on celebrities in lawyer advertisements because the state’s rules aren’t a “blanket prohibition,” as the firm claimed, the Florida Bar said in its first response to the suit.

The bar told a Florida federal court on Friday that Morgan & Morgan lacks standing to sue because it has not yet submitted any celebrity ads to be evaluated under the state’s rule. The firm’s proposed changes to the rule are still being evaluated, the bar said.
The Florida Bar “has a substantial interest in protecting consumers from false, deceptive, misleading, and unduly manipulative lawyer advertising,” it said in the court filing.

Morgan & Morgan, which bills itself as “America’s Largest Injury Law Firm,” sued the Florida Bar in August, arguing the state's ban on celebrities in lawyer ads restricts attorneys’ free speech rights.

The longstanding rule prohibiting lawyers from featuring celebrity images or voices in ads violates the US Constitution's First Amendment and the rule’s definition of celebrities is too vague to be enforceable, Morgan & Morgan said in its complaint. The Florida Bar investigates and prosecutes lawyers for ethics violations in the state.
Attorney Deepak Gupta of Gupta Wessler, who is representing Morgan & Morgan, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday. A Florida Bar spokesperson declined to comment.

Orlando-based Morgan & Morgan is known for its heavy marketing, including television ads and billboards. The ⁠firm spent an estimated $218 million on advertising in 2024, according to the American Tort Reform Association.

In its complaint, Morgan & Morgan said it has developed celebrity advertising campaigns that the firm runs in other ⁠states but cannot feature them in Florida due to the Florida Bar's rule. The firm said it has been prohibited from running advertisements in Florida featuring former NBA star Shaquille O’Neal; actor and race car driver Frankie Muniz; and ⁠professional golfer John Daly.
In its response, the Florida Bar also said it is immune from the lawsuit as an arm of the Supreme Court of Florida, which has sovereign immunity.
